hints: Start by grouping the compounds by functional group. Which two contain a $\text{COOH}$ group and which two contain only an $\text{O-H}$ without a carbonyl?
Recall that carboxylic acids are stronger acids than water and alcohols because the $\text{COO}^-$ anion is stabilised. How does this place water and ethanol relative to the two acids?

Compare ethanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, with butanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. Think about the electron donating effect of a longer alkyl chain on the $\text{O-H}$ bond.
Compare water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, with ethanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. Think about how the ethyl group affects the $\text{O-H}$ bond and the ethoxide anion.
walkthrough:
Sort acids from alcohols and water**
Think about what is left after losing $\text{H}^+$. From $\text{RCOOH}$ you get $\text{RCOO}^-$, where the negative charge is spread over two oxygens by delocalisation. From $\text{ROH}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ you get a localised $\text{RO}^-$ or $\text{OH}^-$. Delocalisation is very stabilising, so both carboxylic acids sit well above water and ethanol in acidity.

Place water above ethanol**
Now look at $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ versus $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. The ethyl group is electron donating by positive inductive effect. It pushes electron density toward the O, which strengthens the $\text{O-H}$ bond making $\text{H}^+$ harder to lose, and it destabilises the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-$ anion by intensifying its negative charge. So water > ethanol.

Place ethanoic acid above butanoic acid**
Apply the same idea to $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ versus $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. The propyl group in butanoic acid is larger and donates more electron density than the methyl group in ethanoic acid. That extra donation strengthens the $\text{O-H}$ bond and destabilises the carboxylate anion more, so butanoic acid is the weaker of the two acids.

Combine into full order**
Putting it together: ethanoic acid (least alkyl donation among acids) > butanoic acid (more alkyl donation) > water (no stabilised carboxylate but no alkyl donation) > ethanol (alkoxide destabilised by ethyl). That is the complete acidity order.

Final answer: ethanoic acid > butanoic acid > water > ethanol (most acidic to least acidic).
Carboxylic acids are stronger due to negative inductive effect of C=O and delocalisation of negative charge over $\text{COO}^-$ stabilising the anion.
Alkyl groups have positive inductive, electron donating effect which strengthens O-H and destabilises anion: propyl in butanoic acid donates more than methyl in ethanoic acid, so butanoic acid is weaker; ethyl in ethanol makes ethanol weaker than water.

hints: Look at the pattern of ticks. Test 1 is positive only for $\text{HCO}_2\text{H}$. Which functional group is present in methanoic acid but absent in the other two acids?
Recall which mild oxidising agent, used warm, oxidises aldehydes but not ketones or ordinary carboxylic acids, giving a silver mirror or brick red precipitate.

Test 2 is positive for $\text{HCO}_2\text{H}$ and $\text{HO}_2\text{CCO}_2\text{H}$ but not for $\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. Which strong warm oxidiser is decolourised by easily oxidised acids like ethanedioic acid?
walkthrough:
Spot the special structure of methanoic acid**
Draw $\text{HCOOH}$ as $\text{H-C(=O)-OH}$. It contains an H attached directly to the carbonyl carbon, just like an aldehyde $\text{H-C(=O)-R}$. Neither $\text{HO}_2\text{CCO}_2\text{H}$ nor $\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ has this. So only methanoic acid can be oxidised by very mild oxidisers.

Assign test 1 as the aldehyde test**
The classic mild test is Tollens reagent, $\text{[Ag(NH}_3\text{)}_2\text{]}^+$, warmed, or Fehlings solution, $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ complex, warmed. With $\text{HCO}_2\text{H}$ you get $\text{Ag}$ as a silver mirror, or $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ as a brick red precipitate. The other two acids give no change, matching row 1: tick, cross, cross.

Assign test 2 as strong oxidation**
Ethanedioic acid, $\text{HOOC-COOH}$, is also easily oxidised to $2\text{CO}_2$, while butanedioic acid with $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2$ between the $\text{COOH}$ groups is resistant. Warm acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ fits: $\text{MnO}_4^-$ (purple) is reduced to $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ (colourless), so the purple colour disappears. Methanoic acid also reduces it, with bubbles of $\text{CO}_2$. That matches row 2: tick, tick, cross.

Final answer: Test 1: Tollens reagent, warm OR Fehling solution, warm; observation: silver mirror OR brick red ppt.
Test 2: acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$, warm; observation: purple colour decolourises (for $\text{HCO}_2\text{H}$ effervescence of $\text{CO}_2$ may also be seen).

hints: For each molecule, label every H and every C, then ask which are related by symmetry. Start with $\text{HCO}_2\text{H}$: are the aldehydic H and the $\text{OH}$ H in the same environment?

For $\text{HO}_2\text{CCO}_2\text{H}$ and $\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, use the centre of symmetry. How many unique $\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{C=O}$ carbon environments remain?
walkthrough:
Count proton environments**
In $\text{HCO}_2\text{H}$, the $\text{H-C=O}$ proton and the $\text{O-H}$ proton are in very different environments, so 2 proton peaks. In $\text{HO}_2\text{CCO}_2\text{H}$, the two $\text{OH}$ protons are identical by symmetry, so 1 proton peak. In $\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, the two $\text{OH}$ protons are identical to each other and the four $\text{CH}_2$ protons are identical to each other by symmetry, so 2 proton peaks ($\text{OH}$ plus $\text{CH}_2$).

Count carbon environments**
In $\text{HCO}_2\text{H}$ there is only one carbon, so 1 carbon peak. In $\text{HO}_2\text{CCO}_2\text{H}$ the two $\text{C=O}$ carbons are symmetric, so 1 carbon peak. In $\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ the two $\text{C=O}$ carbons match each other and the two $\text{CH}_2$ carbons match each other, so 2 carbon peaks.

Final answer: $\text{HCO}_2\text{H}$: proton NMR 2 peaks, carbon-13 NMR 1 peak.
$\text{HO}_2\text{CCO}_2\text{H}$: proton NMR 1 peak, carbon-13 NMR 1 peak.
$\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$: proton NMR 2 peaks, carbon-13 NMR 2 peaks.

hints: Remember what happens to $\text{O-H}$ and $\text{N-H}$ protons when a sample is shaken with $\text{D}_2\text{O}$. Which peak vanishes from the proton NMR spectrum and why?
walkthrough:
Explain the D2O exchange**
Sit with the idea of a labile proton. $\text{COOH}$ protons are acidic and exchange rapidly: $\text{R-O-H + D}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{R-O-D + HOD}$. Deuterium does not appear in a proton NMR spectrum, so the original $\text{OH}$ signal disappears. That disappearance confirms the peak was due to $\text{OH}$.
Final answer: The $\text{OH}$ peak disappears because the labile $\text{OH}$ proton exchanges with deuterium to give $\text{OD}$ which gives no proton NMR signal.

hints: Look at the carbon counts. $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ has 4 carbons, J is a 4 carbon diacid and K is a 6 carbon diamine. Which intermediate must keep 4 carbons and which must gain 2 carbons?
Recall the products of reacting a bromoalkane with $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ versus with $\text{KCN}$. Which gives an alcohol and which adds one carbon per Br as $\text{CN}$?
walkthrough:
Track carbons to assign G and H**
Count carefully. Starting dibromide is $\text{C}_4$. J is $\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, also $\text{C}_4$, so the route G to J must not change carbon number. That fits hydrolysis to a diol then oxidation to a diacid. So G is the $\text{C}_4$ diol: $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$.

Identify the chain extension**
K is $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, which is $\text{C}_6$. The only way to grow from $\text{C}_4$ to $\text{C}_6$ here is cyanide substitution, adding one C per Br. So H is the dinitrile: $\text{NCCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$, which on reduction gives the $\text{C}_6$ diamine.

Final answer: G = $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ (butane-1,4-diol).
H = $\text{NCCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$ (hexanedinitrile).

hints: Step 1 converts $\text{C-Br}$ to $\text{C-OH}$ to make the diol G. What aqueous alkaline reagent and condition hydrolyses bromoalkanes?
Step 2 converts primary alcohol groups in G to carboxylic acid groups in J. Which strong acidified oxidiser, heated, does this?
Step 3 converts $\text{C-Br}$ to $\text{C-CN}$ to make dinitrile H. What cyanide source is used?
Step 4 converts nitrile groups in H to amine groups in K. Which powerful reducing agent reduces nitriles, and what milder alternatives are allowed?
walkthrough:
Step 1, hydrolysis**
You are swapping both Br for OH by nucleophilic substitution. Warm with aqueous sodium hydroxide, $\text{NaOH(aq)}$, gives $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. Do not use ethanolic NaOH, that would favour elimination.

Step 2, oxidation to diacid**
You now need $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ at both ends. That needs a strong oxidiser with heat: acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ with heat, or acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ with heat, under reflux.

Step 3, formation of dinitrile**
You are swapping both Br for CN, again nucleophilic substitution but this time chain extension. Heat with cyanide ion, typically ethanolic $\text{KCN}$ or $\text{NaCN}$: $$\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + 2\text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{NCCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + 2\text{Br}^-$$

Step 4, reduction to diamine**
Finally reduce both $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ to $\text{-CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. The standard reagent is $\text{LiAlH}_4$ in dry ether. Catalytic hydrogenation with $\text{H}_2$/Ni (or Pd, Pt) or Na in ethanol also works: $$\text{NC(CH}_2\text{)}_4\text{CN} + 4\text{[H]} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{N(CH}_2\text{)}_6\text{NH}_2$$

Final answer: step 1: $\text{NaOH(aq)}$, heat.
step 2: acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$, heat OR acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$, heat.
step 3: $\text{KCN}$ / $\text{NaCN}$ / $\text{CN}^-$, heat.
step 4: $\text{LiAlH}_4$ (allow Na in ethanol or $\text{H}_2$ with Ni/Pd/Pt).

hints: Recall that a diacid plus a diamine join by amidation with loss of water. What does the central $\text{-CO-NH-}$ link look like when drawn displayed?

Build the repeat unit from one molecule of J, $\text{HO}_2\text{C(CH}_2\text{)}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, and one of K, $\text{H}_2\text{N(CH}_2\text{)}_6\text{NH}_2$, removing $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Remember to leave free bonds at both ends.
walkthrough:
Form the two amide links**
Picture the condensation: each $\text{COOH}$ loses $\text{OH}$ and each $\text{NH}_2$ loses $\text{H}$ to give $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. The key group to draw displayed is $\text{-C(=O)-N(H)-}$. Getting that carbonyl to NH connection correct earns the first mark.

Assemble the full repeat unit**
Join the carbon skeleton of J, $\text{-CO-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-CO-}$, to the nitrogen skeleton of K, $\text{-NH-(CH}_2\text{)}_6\text{-NH-}$. Draw: $$\text{-[C(=O)-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-NH-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-NH]-}$$ with a trailing bond extending from the first $\text{C}$ and from the last $\text{N}$ to show continuation of the chain.

Final answer: Repeat unit: $\text{-C(=O)-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-NH-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-NH-}$ with trailing bonds at both ends through the outer C and N.
